events.output:
### Manual filtering: file types

Over time, you might notice that you use the same glob patterns over and over.
For example, you might find yourself doing a lot of searches where you only
want to see results for Rust files:

```
$ rg 'fn run' -g '*.rs'
```

Instead of writing out the glob every time, you can use ripgrep's support for
file types:

```
$ rg 'fn run' --type rust
```

or, more succinctly,

```
$ rg 'fn run' -trust
```

The way the `--type` flag functions is simple. It acts as a name that is
assigned to one or more globs that match the relevant files. This lets you
write a single type that might encompass a broad range of file extensions. For
example, if you wanted to search C files, you'd have to check both C source
files and C header files:

```
$ rg 'int main' -g '*.{c,h}'
```

or you could just use the C file type:

```
$ rg 'int main' -tc
```

Just as you can write blacklist globs, you can blacklist file types too:

```
$ rg clap --type-not rust
```

or, more succinctly,

```
$ rg clap -Trust
```

That is, `-t` means "include files of this type" where as `-T` means "exclude
files of this type."

To see the globs that make up a type, run `rg --type-list`:

```
$ rg --type-list | rg '^make:'
make: *.mak, *.mk, GNUmakefile, Gnumakefile, Makefile, gnumakefile, makefile
```

By default, ripgrep comes with a bunch of pre-defined types. Generally, these
types correspond to well known public formats. But you can define your own
types as well. For example, perhaps you frequently search "web" files, which
consist of JavaScript, HTML and CSS:

```
$ rg --type-add 'web:*.html' --type-add 'web:*.css' --type-add 'web:*.js' -tweb title
```

or, more succinctly,

```
$ rg --type-add 'web:*.{html,css,js}' -tweb title
```

The above command defines a new type, `web`, corresponding to the glob
`*.{html,css,js}`. It then applies the new filter with `-tweb` and searches for
the pattern `title`. If you ran

```
$ rg --type-add 'web:*.{html,css,js}' --type-list
```

Then you would see your `web` type show up in the list, even though it is not
part of ripgrep's built-in types.

It is important to stress here that the `--type-add` flag only applies to the
current command. It does not add a new file type and save it somewhere in a
persistent form. If you want a type to be available in every ripgrep command,
then you should either create a shell alias:

```
alias rg="rg --type-add 'web:*.{html,css,js}'"
```

or add `--type-add=web:*.{html,css,js}` to your ripgrep configuration file.
([Configuration files](#configuration-file) are covered in more detail later.)

#### The special `all` file type

A special option supported by the `--type` flag is `all`. `--type all` looks
for a match in any of the supported file types listed by `--type-list`,
including those added on the command line using `--type-add`. It's equivalent
to the command `rg --type agda --type asciidoc --type asm ...`, where `...`
stands for a list of `--type` flags for the rest of the types in `--type-list`.

As an example, let's suppose you have a shell script in your current directory,
`my-shell-script`, which includes a shell library, `my-shell-library.bash`.
Both `rg --type sh` and `rg --type all` would only search for matches in
`my-shell-library.bash`, not `my-shell-script`, because the globs matched
by the `sh` file type don't include files without an extension. On the
other hand, `rg --type-not all` would search `my-shell-script` but not
`my-shell-library.bash`.

### Replacements

ripgrep provides a limited ability to modify its output by replacing matched
text with some other text. This is easiest to explain with an example. Remember
when we searched for the word `fast` in ripgrep's README?

### Configuration file

It is possible that ripgrep's default options aren't suitable in every case.
For that reason, and because shell aliases aren't always convenient, ripgrep
supports configuration files.

Setting up a configuration file is simple. ripgrep will not look in any
predetermined directory for a config file automatically. Instead, you need to
set the `RIPGREP_CONFIG_PATH` environment variable to the file path of your
config file. Once the environment variable is set, open the file and just type
in the flags you want set automatically. There are only two rules for
describing the format of the config file:

1. Every line is a shell argument, after trimming whitespace.
2. Lines starting with `#` (optionally preceded by any amount of whitespace)
are ignored.

In particular, there is no escaping. Each line is given to ripgrep as a single
command line argument verbatim.

Here's an example of a configuration file, which demonstrates some of the
formatting peculiarities:

```
$ cat $HOME/.ripgreprc
# Don't let ripgrep vomit really long lines to my terminal, and show a preview.
--max-columns=150
--max-columns-preview

# Add my 'web' type.
--type-add
web:*.{html,css,js}*

# Search hidden files / directories (e.g. dotfiles) by default
--hidden

# Using glob patterns to include/exclude files or folders
--glob=!.git/*

# or

{"command":"cat > <path> <<'MDEOF'
# Filtering by file type in ripgrep

A *file type* in ripgrep is just a name attached to one or more globs. `rust`
means `*.rs`; `c` means `*.[chH]`, `*.[chH].in` and `*.cats`. Instead of
retyping `-g '*.{c,h}'` on every search, you name the set once and reuse it.
ripgrep ships with just over 200 built-in type definitions, and a handful have
aliases — `py` and `python`, `md` and `markdown`, `ts` and `typescript`,
`bat` and `batch` — so you can spell them the way you think of them.

## `-t/--type`: search only these files

```
$ rg 'fn run' --type rust
$ rg 'fn run' -trust          # short form; the value attaches directly
```

Repeat the flag to widen the net — multiple `-t` flags are OR'd:

```
$ rg TODO -trust -tmd
```

The moment you pass a single `-t`, ripgrep switches into whitelist mode: a file
that matches no selected type is skipped. This is the flag's real value on a
large tree — you are not just filtering output, you are not opening the files
at all.

`--type=all` is a special value meaning "every type currently defined,
including ones you added on this command line." It is whitelist mode over
ripgrep's whole type table: recognized files get searched, unrecognized ones
don't. A shell script named `my-shell-script` with no extension isn't matched
by the `sh` globs, so `-tall` skips it.

If you name a type that doesn't exist, ripgrep errors out rather than quietly
matching nothing — a typo'd `-tpyton` fails loudly.

## `-T/--type-not`: skip these files

```
$ rg clap --type-not rust
$ rg clap -Trust
```

`-T` is the mirror image and also repeatable. The asymmetry worth knowing: `-t`
puts everything else out of scope, while a lone `-T` only removes the named
type and leaves everything else searchable as usual.

You can mix them. When a file matches globs from more than one selection, the
**last one on the command line wins**, so ordering is how you carve out
exceptions:

```
$ rg config -tall -Tjson       # every recognized type except JSON
```

`--type-not=all` is the inverse of `--type=all`: it searches only files ripgrep
*doesn't* recognize. That's a good way to find the strays — extensionless
scripts, odd config files — that your type-based searches have been missing.

## `--type-list`: see what a type actually covers

```
$ rg --type-list | rg '^make:'
make: *.mak, *.mk, GNUmakefile, Gnumakefile, Makefile, gnumakefile, makefile
```

One type per line, name, then `: `, then its globs comma-separated; both the
list and each type's globs are sorted. Reach for this before you assume a type
covers what you think — `js` includes `*.vue`, `*.cjs` and `*.mjs`; `css`
includes `*.scss`; `json` includes `composer.lock`. `--type-list` also reflects
any `--type-add` and `--type-clear` flags in the same invocation, which makes
it the way to check a custom definition before searching with it.

## `--type-add`: define your own

The format is `NAME:GLOB`, one glob per flag, additive to whatever ripgrep
already defines for that name:

```
$ rg title --type-add 'web:*.html' --type-add 'web:*.css' -tweb
$ rg title --type-add 'web:*.{html,css,js}' -tweb        # same thing
```

Defining a type does not select it — you still need `-tweb`.

There is also an include directive that composes existing types:

```
$ rg --type-add 'src:include:cpp,py,md' -tsrc PATTERN
$ rg --type-add 'src:include:cpp,py,md' --type-add 'src:*.foo' -tsrc PATTERN
```

Included types must already be defined by the time the flag is parsed, so put
your `--type-add 'wat:*.wat'` before the `--type-add 'combo:include:wat,py'`
that references it. Type names must be only Unicode letters or numbers — no
punctuation — and `all` is reserved.

The related `--type-clear NAME` wipes a type's globs entirely; you can add new
ones afterward, but `--type-clear rust -trust` with nothing added back is an
error, because `rust` no longer exists.

**None of this persists.** Type settings apply to one invocation only. To keep
a definition, use a shell alias or a config file pointed at by
`RIPGREP_CONFIG_PATH`, one argument per line:

```
--type-add
web:*.{html,css,js}
```

## Things that will bite you

- **Type globs match the file name only, not the path.** `--type-add
  'foo:src/*.rs'` will never match. Use `-g` for path-shaped patterns.
- **Types lose to globs and to ignore files.** Precedence runs `--glob` first,
  then ignore rules, then types. A gitignored file stays unsearched no matter
  what `-t` you pass; add `-u`/`--no-ignore` if you want it back.
- **Explicit paths bypass filtering.** `rg -tpy foo main.rs` searches
  `main.rs`. Type filtering applies to files ripgrep discovers by walking, not
  to ones you hand it.
- **Types never apply to directories,** so `-t` doesn't prune the traversal —
  it prevents files from being read and searched.

## Quick reference

| Flag | Effect |
|---|---|
| `-tTYPE` | search only TYPE (repeatable; whitelist mode) |
| `-t all` | search only recognized types |
| `-TTYPE` | skip TYPE (repeatable) |
| `-T all` | search only unrecognized files |
| `--type-add 'N:GLOB'` | add a glob to type N |
| `--type-add 'N:include:A,B'` | build N from existing types |
| `--type-clear N` | drop N's globs |
| `--type-list` | print all types and their globs |
MDEOF

$ rg --type-add 'src:include:cpp,py,md' --type-add 'src:*.foo' -tsrc PATTERN
```

Included types must already be defined by the time the flag is parsed, so put
your `--type-add 'wat:*.wat'` before the `--type-add 'combo:include:wat,py'`
that references it. Type names must be only Unicode letters or numbers — no
punctuation — and `all` is reserved.

The related `--type-clear NAME` wipes a type's globs entirely; you can add new
ones afterward, but `--type-clear rust -trust` with nothing added back is an
error, because `rust` no longer exists.

**None of this persists.** Type settings apply to one invocation only. To keep
a definition, use a shell alias or a config file pointed at by
`RIPGREP_CONFIG_PATH`, one argument per line:

```
--type-add
web:*.{html,css,js}
```

## Things that will bite you

- **Type globs match the file name only, not the path.** `--type-add
  'foo:src/*.rs'` will never match. Use `-g` for path-shaped patterns.
- **Types lose to globs and to ignore files.** Precedence runs `--glob` first,
  then ignore rules, then types. A gitignored file stays unsearched no matter
  what `-t` you pass; add `-u`/`--no-ignore` if you want it back.
- **Explicit paths bypass filtering.** `rg -tpy foo main.rs` searches
  `main.rs`. Type filtering applies to files ripgrep discovers by walking, not
  to ones you hand it.
- **Types never apply to directories,** so `-t` doesn't prune the traversal —
  it prevents files from being read and searched.

## Quick reference

| Flag | Effect |
|---|---|
| `-tTYPE` | search only TYPE (repeatable; whitelist mode) |
| `-t all` | search only recognized types |
| `-TTYPE` | skip TYPE (repeatable) |
| `-T all` | search only unrecognized files |
| `--type-add 'N:GLOB'` | add a glob to type N |
| `--type-add 'N:include:A,B'` | build N from existing types |
| `--type-clear N` | drop N's globs |
| `--type-list` | print all types and their globs |
